item.title: AI Takes Center Court at the US Open
item.description: [Bloomberg] IBM and the US Open are expanding their use of AI to give fans real-time match insights, including personalized updates, an AI assistant and win probabilities that change after every point. IBM Senior Vice President Jonathan Adashek and former tennis player Sam Querrey are on Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss with hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini how the technology also gives players and coaches deeper data to analyze opponents and match strategy while helping more than 14 million digital users follow the tournament. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Fed Faces High Stakes Test at Jackson Hole
item.description: [Bloomberg] Fed Chair Kevin Warsh heads into Jackson Hole under heightened scrutiny after the Treasury’s intervention in the bond market raised questions about the traditional boundaries between fiscal and monetary policy. Host of Bloomberg Money Tom Keene and Veda Partners Co-Founder Henrietta Treyz are on Bloomberg This Weekend and discuss how investors will be watching for how Warsh addresses inflation, market volatility and Fed independence as economic and geopolitical uncertainty complicate the outlook. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Rep. McCormick Warns Against Slowing AI Buildout
item.description: [Bloomberg] Representative Rich McCormick is on Bloomberg This Weekend with David Gura and Christina Ruffini and says the US should continue expanding data centers to support its leadership in artificial intelligence, arguing they can be built responsibly while benefiting local economies. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Data Center Expansion Tests Voter Patience
item.description: [Bloomberg] The rapid expansion of AI data centers is becoming a political issue in Ohio as residents raise concerns about higher electricity bills, tax incentives and secrecy around local development deals. Representative Greg Landsman joins Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss the issue with hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: How Water Scarcity Is Changing the Economics of the Southwest
item.description: [Bloomberg] The Colorado River provides water to seven states, contributing to an estimated $1.4 trillion in annual economic activity. But decades of decline, record-low snowpack and shrinking reservoirs have pushed the system toward crisis, with Lake Powell nearing levels that could threaten hydropower production. As key rules expire and states fail to reach a long-term deal, the federal government is stepping in with proposed cuts to lower-basin water use, hitting Arizona especially hard. Will the Southwest be able to survive on a shrinking Colorado River? (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Canada Digs In as US Trade Fight Escalates
item.description:
[Bloomberg] Joining Bloomberg This Weekend, Former Canadian Finance Minister Chrystia Freeland says Canada was right to walk away from a trade deal she argues would have harmed both countries, urging Ottawa not to back down and saying past retaliation against US tariffs proved effective. Freeland warns hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that Trump’s approach risks turning allies into “vassals” as Canada prepares dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs after the US imposed new 50% duties.
(This conversation was edited to omit an incorrect statement about the titles of Canadian government officials.) (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: A Teen’s Double Life Reveals London’s Wealth Obsession
item.description: [Bloomberg] Joining Bloomberg This Weekend is Best Selling Author Patrick Radden Keefe to discuss his new book 'London Falling,' which explores the mysterious 2019 death of 19-year-old Zac Brettler, whose parents discovered after his death that he had been posing as the son of a Russian oligarch. Keefe explains to Christina Ruffini that the story examines London’s influx of extreme wealth and social media-fueled status anxiety while tracing a family’s effort to understand the secret life their son had built. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Alliance Tested as Trump Pulls Out of South Korea Drill
item.description: [Bloomberg] The US and South Korea sharply curtailed their annual military exercises after President Donald Trump ordered them scaled back, surprising Seoul as North Korea expands its nuclear and missile capabilities and deepens military ties with Russia. Bloomberg Economics and Senior Geoeconomics Analyst Adam Farrar is on Bloomberg This Weekend with David Gura and Christina Ruffini and explains that move comes as the US shifts an aircraft carrier and other military resources from the Indo-Pacific toward the Middle East, raising questions about Washington’s ability to sustain its security commitments in Asia. item.title: Treasury Buybacks Fail to Calm Bond Market
item.description: [Bloomberg] The Treasury’s surprise decision to at least double buybacks of longer-dated US debt briefly pushed yields lower, but much of that move quickly reversed as investors questioned whether the intervention can overcome inflation and fiscal concerns. PIMCO Executive VP, Market Strategist and Generalist Portfolio Manger Tony Crescenzi and Host of Bloomberg Money Tom Keene join Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss how markets are now looking to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech for clues on rates and how the central bank will respond to Treasury’s increasingly active role in the bond market. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Iceland Faces Close Vote on EU Talks
item.description: [Bloomberg] Iceland will vote August 29th on whether to resume accession talks with the European Union, with recent polling showing a narrow advantage for the “yes” side. RUV Correspondent Ingólfur Bjarni Sigfússon joins Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend and explains that debate is being shaped by security concerns, economic uncertainty and Iceland’s strategic position in the North Atlantic, while opponents warn about sovereignty and control over fisheries. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Can Canada Still Trust America on Trade?
item.description: [Bloomberg] Chrystia Freeland says a tentative US-Canada trade agreement may prevent new US tariffs from taking effect, but only if Canada makes major concessions including easing retaliation, allowing US alcohol back into provincial stores and aligning with Washington on some digital issues. Existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, cars and auto parts would remain, though at lower levels. Freeland says that would mark a major shift from Canada’s long-held position that such tariffs violate USMCA, and could hurt both countries, especially US manufacturing and the Detroit-Windsor auto supply chain. This interview was recorded on Aug. 20. (Source: Bloomberg)
